Analysis plan

A plan for answering each of the questions including the variables involved, variables to be created (if any), external data to be merged in (if any).

Q1. How does the relationship between flipper length and body mass differ among the three penguin species?
With an already clean dataset, no new variables will need to be created. The variables leveraged from the dataset will be body_mass_g, species, and flipper_length_mm. I plan on developing a scatterplot with the body_mass_g and flipper_length_mm on the x and y axis, respectively. Then I would utilize the species variable with a color to observe trends.
Q2. How do the physical proportions of a penguins bill vary between males and females and is the distribution consistent across the three islands?
I will be using the bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, sex, and island to answer this question in a scatterplot. Using bill length on the x axis and depth on the y axis, the sex variable will be mapped ot the color aesthetic and facet_grid() will be used to seperate the data by island.
After receiving feedback, a boxplot option will be explored for q2. The other feedback on how utilizing face_grid() or facet_wrap() will be for the island variable. The functions will create 3 panels for the 3 islands and to observe trends of size gaps between male and females regarding the islands. Also to observe trends regarding bill proportions from each island, seeing if geographic location effects their bills.

title: Morphological Variations in Palmer Penguins
text: This project explores patterns in the Palmer Penguins dataset through data visualization techniques in R and the ggplot2 framework to better understand variation in penguin morphology across species, sex, and island. Two research questions are investigated: (1) how the relationship between flipper length and body mass differs among the three penguin species, and (2) how bill dimensions vary by sex and whether these patterns are consistent across the three islands. Scatterplots, faceted visualizations, and comparative plots are used to reveal trends, correlations, and group differences. The analysis demonstrates that species exhibit distinct relationships between flipper length and body mass, reflecting differences in body size and morphology. Additionally, bill length and bill depth show noticeable variation between males and females, with the magnitude and distribution of these differences differing across islands. Overall, the project highlights how visualization can effectively uncover biological patterns and support exploratory data analysis in ecological datasets.

title: Morphological Variations in Palmer Penguins
text:
Write up

Introduction - Dataset Overview
This analysis utilizes the Palmer Penguins dataset, originally collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER. The dataset consists of 344 observations and 8 variables, serving as a modern, robust foundation for data exploration. It tracks three distinct species of brush-tailed penguins (Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo) across three islands in the Palmer Archipelago (Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen).
This project conducts an exploratory visual analysis of the dataset to uncover physical scaling patterns and geographical distributions without asserting unverified causal claims. By combining numerical metrics (such as body mass, flipper length, and bill dimensions) with categorical demographics (species, sex, and island), this report answers two distinct multivariable questions regarding the ecological structure of these Antarctic communities.


Question 1

Introduction
The first objective of this analysis is to evaluate inter-species scaling by asking: How does the relationship between flipper length and body mass differ among the three penguin species? Due to animals of different species possess unique biological baseline sizes, it is important to observe whether the fundamental relationship between mass and limb length remains consistent across the genus.


Approach
Utilizing 3 key variables defined the approach for this visualization. body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm and species which respectively are numerical and species being categorical. Preparing the data involved dropping any rows containing NA for the previously mentioned variables to ensure a complete visualization could be made. Using the body mass as the x-axis and flipper length as they y-axis was the best approach forward. The species variable gets mapped to both color and shape aesthetics to ensure the clusters are visually distinct. Using a trendline was also another feature to add with geom_smooth to visualize the trajectory of the scaling relationship.


Analysis
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

#load data
df_q1 <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm, species)

#visualization
ggplot(df_q1, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "darkorange", "Chinstrap" = "purple", "Gentoo" = "cyan4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Morphological Scaling by Penguin Species",
    subtitle = "Comparing body mass to flipper length across Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins",
    x = "Body Mass (grams)",
    y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    color = "Species",
    shape = "Species"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )


Discussion
The visualization displays a strong, positive correlation between body mass and flipper length across the entire dataset. The color mapping does highlight some distinct morphological clustering though. The Gentoo penguins exhibit a significantly larger physical profile in comparison to the Adelie and Chinstrap species. Despite the differing sizes, all the dashed linear trend lines demonstrate the same theme of as mass increases. flipper length proportionally increases as well across all three species.



Question 2

Introduction
The second objective transitions into demographic and geographic mapping by asking: How do the physical proportions of a penguin’s bill (length vs. depth) vary between males and females, and is this distribution consistent across the three islands? This evaluates both sexual dimorphism and how regional populations differ across the archipelago.


Approach
This visualization requires the use of four key variables, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, sex, and island. The first two variables being numerical with the latter two being categorical. Filtering out any incomplete entries for the sex variable was required for the data preparation. The x-axis was chosen to be the bill length with the bill dpeth being the y-axis. Sex gets mapped to the color aesthetic and facet_wrap() was utilized to isolate the results from each island. Panel.border and spacing lines were added to reduce any ambiguity and to ensure the results were easy to tell from each island.


Analysis
df_q2 <- penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, sex, island)

#visualization
ggplot(df_q2, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ island) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("female" = "#D95F02", "male" = "#1B9E77")) +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin Bill Proportions by Sex and Island",
    subtitle = "Comparing bill length vs. depth across the Palmer Archipelago",
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
    
  )


Discussion
The faceted scatterplot provides consistent evidence of sexual dimorphism across the Palmer Archipelago. In almost every panel, male observations reliably cluster higher on the y-axis, indicating greater bill depth, than female observations. Furthermore, the geographic faceting reveals stark differences in island populations. While Dream and Torgersen islands feature penguins with relatively short but deep bills which are characteristic of the Adelie and Chinstrap populations, Biscoe Island exhibits a massive, distinct cluster of penguins with long but shallow bills. This visually confirms the localized distribution of Gentoo penguins exclusively on Biscoe Island, proving that their physical traits are closely tied to where they live.

The Question: How does the relationship between a penguin’s body mass and flipper length differ across the three distinct species?


Goal
Seeking to determine if the physical scaling of body mass in comparison to limb length is consistent across the oberserved findings, or if specific species exhibit unique growth trajectories.

Variables Used

Numerical Attributes:

body_mass_g (Independent / X-axis)
flipper_length_mm (Dependent / Y-axis)

Categorical Attribute:

species (Grouping / Color & Shape)

title: Morphological Variations in Palmer Penguins
text:
Question 2: Geography & Dimorphism
The Question: What is the distribution of bill depths across the three islands, and does this change depending on the sex of the penguin?


Goal
This multivariable approach evaluates “Sexual Dimorphism” (size differences between sexes) and whether these physical traits are influenced by the regional island environment.

Variables Used

Numerical Attributes:

bill_depth_mm (Primary Metric / Y-axis)
bill_length_mm (Contextual Metric / X-axis)

Categorical Attributes:

island (Geographic Grouping / Facets)
sex (Biological Grouping / Color)

title: Morphological Variations in Palmer Penguins
text:
Conclusion


1. Interspecies Scaling Answer

Universal Correlation: All three species show a strong, positive relationship between body mass and flipper length.
Consistent Trajectories: While Gentoo penguins are physically larger, their slope is closely identical to the Adelie and Chinstrap populations. This suggests a conserved biological scaling across all observed penguins.


2. Geography & Sex Answer

Sexual Dimorphism: It can be seen that male penguins exhibit greater bill depth than females across all study sites.
Regional Isolation: The visual analysis proves that Gentoo penguins live only only Biscoe Island, making its data physically distinct.


3. Overall

Evolution in Action: Similar to Darwin’s finches, these penguin populations show physical adaptations, bill dimensions, that reflect localized ecological niches.
Narrative Over Noise: By prioritizing data storytelling with a clean dataset, 344 rows of raw metrics were translated into a clear, visual narrative about Antarctic biodiversity.
